The Great Victoria Desert. Australia's largest desert, sprawling roughly one hundred thirty-four thousand square miles across the border of Western Australia and South Australia. Named by the nineteenth-century explorer Ernest Giles in honor of Queen Victoria, it is a vast plateau of red sand, spinifex grassland, and rocky outcrops inhabited by Aboriginal peoples and remarkable desert-adapted wildlife.

The largest desert in Australia and the fifth-largest in the world, it spans nearly two thousand miles east to west and up to four hundred miles north to south. The red soil comes from iron oxide in the ancient Precambrian rocks beneath. It is characterized by a mix of sand dunes, stony plains, and scattered shrubland.

Summer temperatures exceed forty-five degrees Celsius, or one hundred and thirteen degrees Fahrenheit. Rainfall is highly variable and unpredictable, averaging six to eight inches annually, with some years passing without significant precipitation. Aboriginal peoples—including the Martu, Pitjantjatjara, and Ngaanyatjarra—have inhabited and managed the desert for at least forty thousand years via complex knowledge systems.

Named by the explorer Ernest Giles in eighteen seventy-five during his transcontinental journey, European contact profoundly disrupted traditional Aboriginal lifeways. Wildlife includes kangaroos, emus, bearded dragons, and venomous snakes. The ecosystem relies on deep underground aquifers and sporadic rainfall events.

The desert contains sacred Aboriginal sites central to songlines, dreaming stories, and spiritual geography. Land rights remain contested between Aboriginal groups and the Australian state. The Great Victoria comprises three and a half percent of Australia's total area and its largest single desert, representing the ancestral territory and custodianship of Aboriginal inhabitants whose millennia of ecological knowledge remain central to the landscape.
